questions.question: Define drought correctly, explain why the definition must be anchored to the local normal, and set out the four stages of drought in their proper order with the reason for that order.
questions.expected_answer: A drought is an extended period of rainfall well below the average that a particular place normally receives and has organised its life around. The anchor to the local normal is essential because absolute totals mean nothing on their own: Springbok functions on roughly 200 millimetres a year because its farms, tanks and habits are built for it, while the same total would be a catastrophe for Mbombela, which expects nearer 750 millimetres — so drought is below-normal rainfall, never merely low rainfall. The four stages deepen in a fixed order because the shortage physically works its way down from the sky. Meteorological drought is the rainfall shortfall itself. If it persists, agricultural drought follows as soil moisture drops below what crops and grazing need and yields fail. Hydrological drought comes next, when the shortage reaches the storage system — rivers dwindle, dam levels slide and the water table sinks. The final stage is socio-economic drought, when supply can no longer meet human demand and the shortage drives prices, unemployment and migration. One failed season is meteorological; several failed seasons in a row usually means all four stages at once.

questions.question: Explain what desertification is, recite its causal chain, and describe the feedback loop that keeps degraded land degrading, with named examples from Africa and South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Desertification is the degradation of land in arid and semi-arid regions until it behaves like desert — soil stripped of vegetation, structure and nutrients until it can neither store water nor regrow cover. It is not a desert advancing like a wall; it is productive land dying in patches where human pressure is heaviest, with drought exposing the damage rather than causing most of it. The causal chain runs: overgrazing, with herds stripping grass faster than it regrows while hooves compact the soil; over-cultivation, exhausting nutrients and soil structure through cropping without rest; deforestation for fuel and building, leaving soil naked to wind and rain; poor irrigation in hot climates causing salinisation as evaporating water leaves salt behind; and population pressure underneath all four, usually driven by poverty, with climate change intensifying everything. Once cover is lost the physics takes over: bare soil crusts and bakes, rain sheets off in flash floods that cut dongas and strip topsoil, wind lifts the loosened fines as dust, and thinner soil regrows less vegetation, baring more ground — a positive feedback spiral. The Sahel along the Sahara's southern rim is the world's warning region, and South Africa shows the same symptoms on the Karoo margins, the Kalahari fringe and the crowded communal lands of the old Eastern Cape reserves.

questions.question: Describe the Nelson Mandela Bay water crisis as a case study of drought effects, and organise the full range of management strategies into the three families named in the lesson, quoting the named programmes.
questions.expected_answer: From about 2015 the rains repeatedly missed the Eastern Cape catchments feeding Nelson Mandela Bay, and by the winter of 2022 the metro's combined supply dams had sunk toward roughly one-tenth of capacity, with the large Kouga Dam among the worst. Gqeberha prepared collection-point maps for the day the taps failed, throttled mains pressure, chased the large share of supply lost to leaks, drilled emergency boreholes, brought in additional Orange River water through the Nooitgedagt scheme and pushed residents toward fifty litres per person per day. The taps narrowly stayed open until the 2023 rains broke the siege — showing both that the danger was real and that determined management can hold it off. Management falls into three families. See it coming: early warning from rainfall records, Pacific sea temperatures and satellite veld indices layered in a GIS, so relief moves before the peak and farmers destock early, plant drought-tolerant crops and bank fodder. Spend less: water demand management through drip irrigation, night watering and mulching in agriculture — the largest consumer — plus household rainwater harvesting, greywater re-use, steep block tariffs, leak repair and, on the coast, desalination. Heal the land: rotational grazing with realistic stocking rates, crop rotation and cover crops, contour ploughing, check dams in dongas, windbreaks and woodlots, Working for Water clearing thirsty alien invasive trees from catchments while creating jobs, LandCare rehabilitating communal land, and the Great Green Wall carrying village-led restoration across the Sahel from Senegal to Djibouti.
